questions.q: Define "narrative unreliability" in first-person autobiographical fiction and give one example from "vkyks&vk¡èkkfj" where the protagonist's self-reporting contradicts textual evidence.
questions.a: Narrative unreliability occurs when a first-person narrator's account is compromised by limited self-awareness, emotional bias, or intentional self-justification, creating a gap between what the narrator claims and what the text's details reveal. In "vkyks&vk¡èkkfj," the protagonist repeatedly asserts "eq>s dke osQ ckjs esa oqQN ugha tkurh" (I know nothing about work matters) while simultaneously managing complex household budgets, negotiating wages, and strategically changing employers—evidence that she possesses significant practical intelligence she disavows. A wrong answer that merely identifies her as "honest" or "simple" reveals the student confuses the narrator's *self-presentation* with the author's *characterization*, missing Chandrakanta's deliberate irony.

questions.q: Explain in your own words how the recurring motif of "keys" (ckFk:e, tk¡p, dj.k) functions as a structural metaphor for the protagonist's evolving agency across the narrative.
questions.a: Keys initially symbolize the protagonist's *exclusion*—she carries employers' keys but never owns a key to her own space (pages 22-23: "ckFk:e dh vlqfoèkk ugha Fkh"). Mid-narrative, keys become instruments of *negotiated access*—she duplicates keys to move between households efficiently, turning employers' property into her mobility tool. In the climax, the key metaphor inverts: she gifts rkrq'k a diary with its own lock ("fp_h dksydkrk"), claiming the power to lock/unlock her own story. A wrong answer listing key references without tracing the *progression* from passive to active agency reveals the student treats motifs as static symbols rather than dynamic structural devices that evolve with character arc.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "double voicing" (Bakhtin) to analyze the scene where the protagonist teaches the employer's children to read while remaining illiterate herself (pages 24-25). Write a 4-sentence analysis identifying both voices and their tension.
questions.a: The scene operates in double voice: the *dominant voice* is the employer's liberal rhetoric ("cPpksa dks i<+kbZ&fy[kkbZ dh njdkj gS") which frames education as universal right; the *subaltern voice* is the protagonist's embodied reality ("esjk i<+uk&fy[kuk Hkh ugha gks ldk") where education is a privilege extracted from her labor. The tension erupts when she performs the teacher's role—holding chalk, guiding fingers—while her own fingers remain "v[kckj" (ink-stained) from domestic work. This isn't mere irony; it's structural violence made visible: the literacy she enables for others is built on the illiteracy enforced upon her. A wrong answer that calls this "sad" or "unfair" without naming the *two competing discourses* reveals the student cannot distinguish thematic observation from discursive analysis.

questions.q: Compare the protagonist's relationship with rkrq'k (the male employer who mentors her writing) and lquhy (the female employer who exploits her). Analyze how the text uses gendered power dynamics to complicate the "savior" narrative.
questions.a: rkrq'k and lquhy represent two faces of patriarchal control: lquhy exercises *direct domination* through physical surveillance, wage theft, and bodily control (locking her in, monitoring bathroom use); rkrq'k exercises *benevolent paternalism* through "mentorship" that extracts intellectual labor (publishing her work under his guidance, controlling her literary access). Crucially, the text refuses to romanticize rkrq'k—his final demand that she send her son away for "better opportunities" (page 50) mirrors lquhy's family separation, revealing both men as agents of the same system. The protagonist's breakthrough comes not through either man but through *rejecting both frameworks* when she claims "esjs fy[kkoV igys eq>s dkI+kQh d"V nsrh Fkh. vc d"V nsus dh ckr rks nwj" (page 50). A wrong answer praising rkrq'k as "the good employer" reveals the student reads character intentions literally rather than analyzing structural positioning.

questions.q: Evaluate the critical claim: "The protagonist's authorship at the novel's end represents genuine liberation, not co-optation." Defend or challenge using three textual evidences from the final 10 pages.
questions.a: The claim is *partially defensible but incomplete*. Evidence for liberation: (1) She physically possesses her manuscript ("fp_h fy[kus dk flj&iSj eSa tkurh ugha Fkh fiQj Hkh tSls cu iM+k fy[kk"), (2) She rejects rkrq'k's editorial control ("rkrq'k us dgk] rqEgsa bu lc ckrksa dks ysdj vHkh ekFkk&iPph djus dh ”k:jr ugha gSA rqe viuk dke fd, tkvks"), (3) She frames writing as intergenerational gift ("ge nksuksa tc ,d nwljs ls feysaxs rks th&Hkjdj g¡lsaxs"). Evidence for co-optation: (1) Her publication depends on rkrq'k's connections ("rkrq'k osQ ikl ls ,d caèkq osQ ikl dksydkrk Hkst fn;k"), (2) The publisher's contract demands "eksM+ rd igq¡pkuk" (compromise), (3) The final image of her writing "tsBw dh ftruh fpf_;k¡ vkrha mruh esjh bPNk gksrh" suggests her labor still fuels male creativity. The synthesis: liberation is *contested and conditional*, not absolute. A wrong answer taking a binary stance ("yes she's free" or "no she's trapped") reveals the student cannot hold dialectical complexity—a core requirement for Class 11 critical analysis.
